### Do I have to pay for commercial use? 

No. You are not required to pay for a commercial license, however if you are using Obsidian for work in an organization we encourage you to purchase a commercial license to keep Obsidian independent and 100% user-supported. Learn more.

### Can I buy Obsidian add-ons or licenses for someone else? 

Yes! You can purchase Obsidian Credit for friends, family, and coworkers. This credit can be used to pay for any Obsidian license or service. To get started, create an account and buy credit. You can then send it to the recipient via email or a shareable link. Learn more. 

### What is your refund policy? 

We offer full refunds within 7 days of purchase with no questions asked for Obsidian Sync and Publish. However, please note that Catalyst licenses, Commercial licenses, and Obsidian Credit are non-refundable. Learn more.

title: What Obsidian actually costs in 2026, the real numbers
text:
The moment you want the same vault on your phone and your laptop, the free plan stops covering it. Obsidian doesn’t sync accounts by default. That’s a separate product called Obsidian Sync, at $4 a month per user billed annually, or $5 a month billed monthly. It covers syncing your vault across devices, end-to-end encryption, version history, the ability to collaborate on a shared vault with someone else, and priority support.

For a single person who just wants their notes on two devices, that’s $48 a year on the annual rate: a real, recurring cost for what many other apps in this category treat as a baseline feature rather than an upsell.

...

Publish is a different add-on again, aimed at people who want to turn some or all of a vault into a website, a public wiki, documentation, or a digital garden. It costs $8 a month per site billed annually, or $10 a month billed monthly, and includes a customisable theme, graph view and full-text search on the published site, with no separate hosting to arrange.

...

Catalyst is a one-off $25 payment, not a subscription. It funds development ahead of general release and gets you early access to beta builds and some community extras. It doesn’t unlock Sync or Publish, and it isn’t required to use anything in the free app.

Commercial licence is $50 per user, per year, and it’s aimed at organisations that want to support development, not a requirement for using the app at work. Obsidian’s own licence page states plainly that the free app is free for all purposes, including commercial use, non-profits, schools and government bodies, no account or payment required. Buying a Commercial licence gets an organisation listed as a supporter; it doesn’t unlock anything the free app can’t already do. Students, faculty and nonprofit employees separately get 40% off Sync and Publish.

## What it actually costs, for the sizes people actually are

- One person, one device, notes only: free, indefinitely, no catch.
- One person, two or more devices: $48 a year for Sync (annual rate), or $60 a year paying monthly.
- One person who also wants to publish a note publicly: add Publish on top: $96 a year annually, or $120 monthly, for $144 a year total alongside Sync.
- A small team sharing a vault, at work: Sync per seat if you want cross-device syncing, same as anyone else. A Commercial licence ($50 a year per seat) is optional, there to support development, not a requirement for using Obsidian in a business.

title: Notion vs Obsidian vs Coda for Solo Founders (2026) - The Real AI Operator
text:
- Pick Notion if you want one place for docs, tasks, CRM, and a wiki. It’s cloud-only, and per-seat pricing adds up the second you bring in collaborators. I use it every day, for what that’s worth.
- Pick Obsidian if you write a lot and your notes are how you think. Everything lives on your own machine. No subscription, no lock-in, no third party deciding whether you still have access tomorrow.
- Pick Coda if ops is what’s eating your week. It turns pipelines, trackers, and internal tools into docs you can maintain without paging a developer.

...

### Obsidian: local-first notes with a graph

I haven’t shipped Obsidian into my own stack. What follows comes from vendor docs, public reviews on G2 and Capterra, and helping a few friends set it up. Treat that as the caveat.

Obsidian is a desktop and mobile app that stores every note as a plain Markdown file in a folder on your device. No server, no account, no monthly fee for the app itself. The standout features are bidirectional links (write `[[idea name]]` and Obsidian auto-connects notes) and a graph view that shows your notes as a constellation of dots. There’s also a plugin ecosystem of roughly 2,000 community extensions that can turn the app into a task manager, a CRM, a journal, or some Frankenstein combo of all three.

Obsidian is the only one of the three that’s genuinely free for commercial use. The two paid add-ons are Obsidian Sync at $4 per user per month, billed annually, for cross-device sync, and Obsidian Publish for turning notes into a public site. A third tier called Catalyst ($50 or $100 one-time) is a donation track that unlocks early access features.

The honest trade: community threads are full of solo founders who bounced off Obsidian after a week because the graph view looks great in screenshots and useless for actual work. The plugin rabbit hole makes it worse. You’ll spend a Sunday configuring Dataview instead of shipping anything.

...

| Feature | Notion | Obsidian | Coda |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Storage model | Cloud-only | Local Markdown files | Cloud (with offline editing) |
| Best for | Docs + tasks + wiki in one | Thinking, writing, knowledge base | Operations, trackers, internal tools |
| Pricing entry point | Free / Plus $12 per user per month | Free / Sync $4 per user per month | Free / Pro $10 per Doc Maker per month |
| Offline mode | Limited (recent pages only) | Full. It is a desktop app | Partial (edits sync when reconnected) |
| Database / tables | Yes (six view types) | Via plugins (Dataview) | Yes (the core feature) |
| Automations | Built-in (Notion Automations) | Via plugins | Built-in (Buttons + Packs) |
| AI features | Notion AI on every paid plan | Via plugins (Copilot, Smart Connections) | Coda Brain included on Pro |
| Public sharing | Yes (with Notion Sites) | Yes (with Publish add-on) | Yes (free) |
| Mobile apps | iOS, Android | iOS, Android (free; Sync is the paid add-on) | iOS, Android |
| Open data export | CSV / Markdown export | Already Markdown (yours forever) | CSV / Doc export |
| Learning curve | Medium (1-2 weeks) | Low for notes, high for plugin setup | Medium-high (it is a builder) |

...

### Running a content calendar

Notion wins this. I’ve set up content calendars in Notion for myself and for clients, and it’s still the cleanest option. Status, owner, publish date, and the brief all sit in the same row. Filter by status, group by channel, drag a card from Draft to Published, and your VA can run it without a walkthrough. Coda can match it and has heavier table logic under the hood, but the UX is denser. Handing it to a non-technical contractor means more explaining. Obsidian can do it with the Kanban plugin and Dataview, but you’re basically rebuilding the wheel yourself.

### Writing your weekly investor update

Obsidian wins this one for people who think by writing. The weekly update is mostly prose, and Obsidian’s `[[link]]` syntax lets you reference a customer or a metric from any past note without leaving the keyboard. The reason it works: it’s a native desktop app reading and writing plain markdown files. No page reloads, no block-by-block loading. Notion handles it fine but those reloads interrupt long-form flow in a way a native app does not. Coda is the worst pick here because buttons and tables crowd the writing surface.

...

## Pricing for a one-person company

What you pay boils down to two things: how many people touch the workspace and which features you actually use. Here’s what a solo founder sees in August 2026.

- Notion: Free for personal use. Plus runs $10 per member per month on annual billing ($12 if you go monthly). Most solo folks stay on Free until they hit the file upload cap or need longer page history.
- Obsidian: The desktop app is free on every platform. If you want your iPad and phone to stay in sync, add Obsidian Sync at $4 a month, billed annually.
- Coda: Free for unlimited viewers. Pro is $10 per Doc Maker per month on annual billing. Most solo founders stick with Free because there’s only one of you editing.

The catch nobody mentions upfront: Notion bills per member, including people who just read. Coda bills per Doc Maker. So if you share your workspace with five advisors who only read, Notion charges you for six seats. Coda charges you for one. I set up a Notion workspace for a client a while back and handed out a few guest logins without thinking too hard about it. The bill at the end of the month made me wince.

Flip the math to a 20-person team and it reverses. Notion’s flat per-seat pricing usually beats Coda’s free-viewer play once everyone’s actively editing. So don’t pick on pricing alone. Look at who’s actually writing in the doc versus who’s just lurking.

...

### Obsidian’s gotchas

- No real-time collaboration. If two people need to edit the same note at the same time, this isn’t the tool.
- Sync is end-to-end encrypted but it’s a separate paid product. Desktop and mobile apps are free, only Sync costs money.
- The plugin ecosystem is a trap. You will burn a Saturday installing fourteen plugins to “build the perfect system.” Community threads are full of people who’ve fallen into this.

...

## What I’d pick if I were starting over today

For a solo founder starting from scratch, no cofounder, no team, just you and the work, I’d start with Notion Free. It’s what I use for my own company wiki, CRM, and task board. Day-one basics for a one-person company, and Notion ships them out of the box.

When thinking work starts crowding out the operations stuff, research, interview transcripts, half-formed ideas you’d never put in a wiki, that’s when I’d add Obsidian on the side. What I saw going through the docs and community threads: it’s local-first, files are plain markdown, no lock-in. That second part matters more than people realize. If you ever want to bail, your notes are just .md files on disk. Notion handles the structured deliverables. Obsidian handles the thinking. They don’t compete. Tradeoff: cross-device sync isn’t free, and the plugin setup has a learning curve. For a founder buried in notes though, it earns its keep.

title: Notion vs Obsidian for Solopreneurs: Pick by the Job (2026)
text:
## The short answer

Pick Notion if most of what you track has a status, a due date or a price: content calendars, launch checklists, product lists, a simple sales pipeline. Its databases and its free calendar app do that work, and the Free plan lists unlimited blocks for a single user.

Pick Obsidian if most of what you produce is writing and thinking: research notes, scripts, newsletter drafts, a long-lived idea file. Your notes stay as Markdown files in a folder on your own machine, and the app is free for business use.

If you do both kinds of work heavily, run both. Give each job one home. That last rule matters more than the choice itself.

...

| Job in a one-person business | Better fit | Why | What decides it (as of October 2026) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Content calendar with statuses | Notion | Database views by date and status; dates show in Notion Calendar | Notion Calendar is free and can show dates from Notion databases |
| Launch or product tracker | Notion | Relations, properties, buttons | Free plan automations are buttons only; custom database automations start on Plus |
| Intake form (feedback, waitlist, sponsor inquiries) | Notion | Forms write straight into a database | Free has basic forms; custom forms on Plus, conditional logic on Business |
| SOP library you’ll reread for years | Obsidian | Plain files outlive any vendor | Notes are Markdown text files in a local folder |
| Research and swipe file | Obsidian | Fast local search, linking between notes | No plan needed; personal and commercial use are free |
| Long-form drafts (scripts, ebooks, newsletters) | Obsidian | Distraction-light editor, files you can open anywhere | Same Markdown files work in any editor |
| Simple tables over your own notes | Either | Obsidian Bases now gives table, list, cards, kanban and map views | Bases is a core plugin; the data stays in your Markdown files |
| Public help page, roadmap or link hub | Notion for speed, Obsidian for a real site | Notion pages can be shared; Obsidian Publish builds a site with custom domain and passwords | Publish is $8 per site per month billed yearly |
| Asking an AI assistant about your notes | Notion if you’ll pay for Business; Obsidian if your AI tool reads local files | Notion AI is a Business feature; Notion MCP lets outside AI apps in | Free and Plus get a limited AI trial only; MCP connects Claude, Cursor and ChatGPT Pro |
| Capturing ideas from your phone | Either, with a caveat for Obsidian | Notion syncs by default; Obsidian needs a sync method | Free iCloud sync is supported only between Apple devices |

...

Obsidian’s case is ownership. Your SOPs, research and drafts are text files in a folder you control, which means any backup tool, any editor and any script can work with them. For notes you expect to reread in five years, that’s the safer bet.

The licence question is settled, and plenty of older articles still get it wrong. Obsidian’s license terms, last updated February 20, 2025, say the app is free for all purposes, personal, commercial and non-profit. The $50-per-user yearly commercial license is optional, a way to support the company.

Obsidian also closed part of the database gap. Bases is a core plugin that builds database-like views of your notes, with table, list, cards, kanban and map layouts, and the data stays in your Markdown files and their properties. It won’t replace Notion’s forms or calendar sync. It does mean a book list, a product inventory or a simple content log no longer forces you into Notion.

...

## What one person actually pays, October 2026

Most comparisons list plan prices without saying which ones a solo operator would actually buy. The table below prices the realistic setups for one person, collected from the official pricing and help pages on October 19, 2026.

| Setup for one person | Monthly cost | Billed yearly | The limit you’ll hit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Notion Free | $0 | $0 | 5 MB per file, 7-day page history, AI trial only |
| Notion Plus | $10 listed per member | Up to 20% off yearly | Notion AI still trial-only |
| Notion Business (for Notion AI) | $20 listed per member | Up to 20% off yearly | AI usage allowance is included, but premium models use Notion credits |
| Obsidian, no add-ons | $0 | $0 | You handle sync yourself |
| Obsidian + Sync Standard | $5 | $4/month | 1 GB total, 5 MB per file, 1 synced vault, 1 month of history |
| Obsidian + Sync Plus | $10 | $8/month | 10 GB (upgradable to 100 GB), 200 MB per file, 10 vaults, 12 months of history |
| Add Obsidian Publish | +$10 per site | +$8/month per site | One site per subscription |
| Optional Obsidian commercial license | n/a | $50 per user per year | Not required for business use |

Notion’s pricing page lists Plus at $10 and Business at $20 per member a month and says yearly billing saves up to 20%, but it doesn’t label which billing period the headline figure assumes. Check the toggle at checkout before you commit to a year.

The practical read: a solo writer on Obsidian with Sync Standard pays $48 a year. A solo operator who wants AI inside Notion pays the Business rate. Everything in between depends on whether your notes include large files.

...

## Running both without double entry

A split setup works when the boundary is a rule, not a mood. Here’s the one that holds up for a solo business:

- Anything with a date, status or price goes in Notion.
- Anything you write or think through goes in Obsidian.
- When a draft ships, the Notion row gets a link or a file path to it. The text itself never moves.

Don’t mirror notes between the two. The moment you’re copying the same paragraph into both apps, you’ve built a second job for yourself. If you’re still assembling the rest of your tools, the tool stack category and our roundup of AI tools for solopreneurs cover the other pieces.

Your next step: write down the three jobs from the use-case table you do every single week, and count which app wins two of the three. Set up only that app this week, move only those three jobs into it, and don’t touch the other app for 14 days.

title: Notion vs Obsidian: Best Knowledge Base for Solo Operators and Lean Teams
text:
Quick answer: Notion wins for team collaboration, structured workspaces, and shared knowledge. Obsidian wins for solo knowledge workers who care about longevity, ownership, and the durability of a local-first file format that won’t disappear if a vendor pivots.

...

## Pricing breakdown

Notion Free is generous for personal use; Plus is $8/user/month, Business is $15/user/month. Notion AI is +$8/user/month. Obsidian is free for personal use; commercial use requires a $50/user/year license. Obsidian Sync is $4/month, Publish is $8/month. Total cost for serious solo use: Notion $96-$192/year; Obsidian $48-$144/year. Roughly half.

One thing the headline pricing rarely captures: time-cost. The cheaper tool can be the more expensive one once you factor in setup hours, training, integration work, and the productivity loss while your team adapts. For a 10-person team, even a $50/month savings is dwarfed by a single week of slower onboarding. Run the math on total cost, not list price.

...

The solo founder who wants to ship now. Pick the tool with the lower setup tax. Whichever of Notion or Obsidian you can have running in an afternoon is the right answer at this stage. Optimize for speed-to-value; you can migrate later if you outgrow it. Don’t pre-optimize for a team you don’t have yet.

The 10-person team consolidating tools. The right pick is the one that replaces the most existing subscriptions without losing workflows that are already working. Audit what your team uses today, score how each candidate covers those use cases, and add a one-month parallel run to your decision plan before fully cutting over. Tool transitions burn weeks if rushed.

title: Obsidian Review 2026: Free Markdown Notes Worth It?
text:
## Obsidian pricing in 2026: still mostly free

Obsidian's pricing model is unusually generous for a SaaS company: the core app is free for personal and commercial use, forever. You only pay if you want one of three optional services.

$0 Core app, all platforms

~$4-5/mo Obsidian Sync (verify on site)

~$8-10/mo Obsidian Publish (verify on site)

1,500+ Community plugins available

- Obsidian Sync — E2E-encrypted cloud sync across desktop and mobile. Useful if you don't trust third-party sync tools. Pricing has historically been a flat monthly fee per user, with a free trial for new accounts. Confirm current rate at obsidian.md.
- Obsidian Publish — Publish a curated subset of your vault as a static website at a custom domain. Great for digital gardens, research blogs, or documentation.
- Obsidian Catalyst — A one-time payment that unlocks insider builds and funds development. No recurring fees, no feature gating forever — it is essentially a tip jar with perks.

You can use 100% of Obsidian's note-taking features, including plugins and themes, for free. That is a remarkable position in 2026, when most "AI-powered" note apps charge $10–$20/month for the basics.

...

### ✓ Use Obsidian if you:

- Want your notes in plain Markdown you can read in 10 years.
- Enjoy tinkering with plugins, themes, and CSS snippets.
- Do solo research, writing, journaling, or studying.
- Care about offline access and not being at a vendor's mercy.
- Already use (or want to use) a graph-style "second brain" workflow.

...

- Need real-time multi-user editing with a small team.

...

- Prefer Apple-native apps and live entirely in the iCloud ecosystem.
- Need a built-in CRM, kanban, or database tool with rich relations.
- Get frustrated by configuration menus and reading documentation.

...

## Obsidian pricing

 Verified May 2026. Vendor's published rates at the time we checked — always confirm at checkout. 

Obsidian pricing tiers

| Plan | Price | Term | What you get |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Free | Free | forever | Full local note-taking, no sign-up required, unlimited notes |
| Sync | $4/user/mo | annual | $5/mo monthly; end-to-end encrypted sync across devices, version history, shared vaults |
| Publish | $8/site/mo | annual | $10/mo monthly; publish notes as a website with custom themes and graph view |
| Catalyst | $25 | one-time | Early beta access, community badges — supports development |
| Commercial | $50/user/year | annual | Required for commercial use in organizations |
